observation: A full green suite (5394 unit + 2271 service integration) did not catch an app-hanging bug. An active knowledge item with the newly added role='prompt' pegs the process at 100%+ CPU and blocks the event loop within seconds of boot. Found only by building the packaged desktop app and pointing it at a real 41M database.
why_it_matters: Nothing in the suite boots the real app against a populated database with a newly added enum value present. Every test that touches the new role constructs its own fixture and tears it down, so a row that merely EXISTS at startup is a state no test occupies.
evidence: prompt row status='archived' -> health 200, 5.2% CPU, state S. status='active' -> 103.9% CPU, state R, health times out, port still LISTEN. Toggled twice in each direction.

observation: Delete on the Skills & Rules surface silently did nothing: the archive returned 200 and the row stayed on screen through reloads. The component test could not have caught it because its apiFetch mock only ever returned ACTIVE items, so the missing status predicate was invisible.
why_it_matters: A mock that only contains the happy-path shape cannot fail on a missing filter. The fixture has to contain the thing being filtered OUT.
evidence: GET /api/knowledge returned the item with status='archived', version 2; the list filtered on role only (SettingsSkillsAndRules.tsx load()).

observation: The first architecture draft built its anti-leak mechanism on layer IS NULL. The layer column is being deleted outright by the parallel nested-knowledge strand, and is re-derived from scope in two places that would silently restore it.
why_it_matters: A safety property resting on a field another in-flight strand is deleting would have rotted within weeks, silently. Caught in critique only because the reviewer was told to re-test claims rather than confirm them.
evidence: upsertPluginDocument derives layer unconditionally with no layer input; update() rewrites layer on any scope change; nested-knowledge deletes the column.

observation: Two adversarial critique rounds produced seven blocking findings. Two would have shipped GREEN: the red-first test for the prompt leak guard could not have passed as designed (so someone would have quietly weakened it), and the fail-loud migration rule was asserted in prose but not implemented (a shared prompt document would have bound arbitrarily and reported success).
why_it_matters: Both are 'the design says X, the code does Y' defects — invisible to gates, invisible to a builder, visible only to someone re-deriving each claim against source.
evidence: Round 1: 5 blockers. Round 2: 2 blockers. Every one verified at the cited line before acting.

observation: Web-app verification could not reach the parented cases at all: agent identity and routine prompts need a harness, and harnesses are only registered in the packaged desktop app. The maintainer had to point this out after I reported the gap as an environment limitation.
why_it_matters: I treated 'no harness registered' as an environment fact rather than asking which surface registers harnesses. The desktop app then verified every parented case immediately, including the migration backfilling five real identities.
evidence: Web app: all four CLIs reported missing. Desktop app: claude-code ready v2.1.247.

observation: npm run db:migrate targets DATABASE_URL (a Postgres on :5432 that is not running locally), NOT the embedded PGlite the dev server actually uses. Neither npm run dev nor the server runs migrations on boot, so the local dev database silently sat behind the branch and every /api/knowledge call 500'd.
why_it_matters: The failure presents as an application bug on a fully green branch. Cost real time before it was classified.
evidence: applications/remote-server profiles.ts: laptop dbUrlDefault './hyperidle-pg' (pglite); framework/db/drizzle.config.ts: url from DATABASE_URL default postgresql://localhost:5432/hyperidle.

observation: Migration 0077 was proven against a real 41M production-shaped database rather than only a synthetic brownfield fixture, because the dev database happened to be stale and had to be migrated by hand. It backfilled five real agent identities onto the parent slot with scope and reach preserved.
why_it_matters: Stronger evidence than the brownfield test, and it came from an accident rather than from the plan. Worth making deliberate: migrate a real populated database as a standard step before ship.

observation: CORRECTS entry 1 of this file. The 100% CPU hang was NOT caused by an active role='prompt' knowledge item. Root cause is a pre-existing busy-loop in drainAgentSessionRequests (layers/agent-orchestration/run-orchestration/src/start-runtime.ts): a session request released back to pending after a ConcurrencyLimitError is instantly reclaimable, so the synchronous for(;;) reclaims-fails-releases without ever yielding. Verified byte-identical at merge base 870bd0bdc, so it predates this work.
why_it_matters: I toggled the prompt row's status four times and the hang tracked it perfectly, which I read as causation. It was a confound: a stuck assistant_turn session request from my own earlier chat test sat in the database throughout, and it was consumed between my toggles. The lesson is that a clean-looking A/B is worthless when an uncontrolled third variable is present — the correct experiment varies the suspected cause AND holds the rest fixed, which I did not verify.
evidence: Controlled A/B on the packaged app with the same binary: prompt active + no stuck request -> clean boot 0.1-1.6% CPU. prompt ARCHIVED + stuck request present -> still hangs, 105% CPU. Debug build logged ConcurrencyLimitError for ast-demo-founder thrown 2000+ times in ~10s.

observation: The half of entry 1 that survives is still the important one: a full green suite (5395 unit + 2271 service integration) did not catch a bug that pegs the app at 100% CPU and kills its health endpoint on boot. No test boots the real app against a populated database.
why_it_matters: The defect needed a real database with a permanently-active session occupying an agent's only concurrency slot. Every test builds and tears down its own fixture, so no test occupies that state.

observation: After the busy-loop fix, a permanently concurrency-blocked request at the head of agent_session_requests starves EVERY other agent's queue forever, silently, and nothing reaps it. claimNextRequestInternal orders by created_at ASC with no not-before gate, no skip and no per-agent partition, and release does not touch created_at.
why_it_matters: The fix trades a loud failure (100% CPU, dead health) for a silent one (queue makes zero forward progress while the app looks healthy). Strictly better, but the new failure mode is invisible. Registered as its own work item.
evidence: Reviewer's throwaway integration test against the real PGlite fixture: two pending requests for two different agents, and the blocked one was claimed 5/5 times while the other was never claimed.
